title: Browse Dual Special Needs plans
summary: Explains UnitedHealthcare Dual Special Needs plans (D-SNPs): who they are for, benefits, eligibility, costs, availability, and how they differ from other Special Needs plans.

atoms.title: What a Dual Special Needs plan is
atoms.question: What is a Dual Special Needs plan?
atoms.text: A Dual Special Needs plan (D-SNP) is for people who have both Medicare and Medicaid coverage. It combines Medicare Part A and Part B benefits, plus prescription drug coverage and support to help coordinate benefits with Medicaid.

atoms.title: Benefits of UnitedHealthcare Dual Complete plans
atoms.question: What benefits can a UnitedHealthcare D-SNP include?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare says it is America's most chosen brand for Dual Special Needs plans, based on total D-SNP enrollment from CMS data, May 2025. A Dual Complete plan may include monthly premiums as low as $0, $0 annual physical exams, lab tests and preventive care, $0 copays for Tier 1 prescriptions, a monthly credit for OTC products, healthy food and utilities for qualifying members, and $0 copay on vision and hearing exams. Some benefits may also be available from a state Medicaid program or managed Medicaid plan.

atoms.title: Who a D-SNP is and isn't right for
atoms.question: Who should choose a D-SNP?
atoms.text: A D-SNP may be right for you if you have Medicare and Medicaid, need help to coordinate your care, and want extra benefits along with what you receive from Medicaid. It may not be right if you qualify for either Medicare or Medicaid but not both, you live outside an eligible plan coverage area, or another plan type, such as a Chronic Special Needs plan, better fits your needs.

atoms.title: C-SNPs, I-SNPs and IE-SNPs explained
atoms.question: What other Special Needs plans are available besides D-SNPs?
atoms.text: Chronic Special Needs plans (C-SNPs) help people manage severe or disabling long-term health conditions; UnitedHealthcare offers C-SNPs for people with diabetes, chronic heart failure and/or cardiovascular disorders. Institutional Special Needs plans (I-SNPs) are for people who live in a long term care setting, such as a skilled nursing facility. Institutional Equivalent Special Needs plans (IE-SNPs) are for people who receive skilled nursing care at home or in assisted living. All SNPs include prescription drug coverage.

atoms.title: Extra benefits a D-SNP may offer
atoms.question: What does a D-SNP cover?
atoms.text: D-SNPs offer extra Medicare benefits that may include dental, vision and hearing coverage, personalized care coordination, telehealth virtual doctor visits, credits to buy health products, and transportation assistance.

atoms.title: Medicare versus Medicaid
atoms.question: What is the difference between Medicare and Medicaid?
atoms.text: Medicare is a federal health insurance program intended to serve people who are 65 or older, or have a qualifying disability or medical condition. Medicaid is a joint federal and state government program that helps pay health care costs for people with limited income and resources, and Medicaid plans vary from state to state. You may qualify for both based on your health and income level, and people who are dual eligible can often qualify for a D-SNP.

atoms.title: Medicare and Medicaid eligibility requirements
atoms.question: How do I know if I'm eligible for Medicare and Medicaid?
atoms.text: To qualify for Medicare benefits you must be a U.S. citizen or have been a legal resident for at least five years, be 65 years old or have a qualifying disability if younger than 65, and have worked and paid Social Security taxes for at least 10 years (40 quarters). To qualify for Medicaid services you must have an income level within your state's income threshold, live within the state where you apply, have a Social Security number, and be a U.S. citizen or meet immigration requirements.

atoms.title: How much a D-SNP costs
atoms.question: How much does a D-SNP cost?
atoms.text: D-SNP costs depend on the plan you choose and on your level of Medicaid eligibility. Financial support from Medicaid helps cover out-of-pocket costs for expenses like premiums, copayments, coinsurance and deductibles. Dual Special Needs plans have a $0 premium for members with Extra Help (Low Income Subsidy) from Medicare.

atoms.title: Where D-SNPs are available
atoms.question: Is a UnitedHealthcare D-SNP available where I live?
atoms.text: Probably. D-SNPs are available from private insurance companies in 46 states and the District of Columbia. They are not available in Alaska, Illinois, New Hampshire or Vermont. If a D-SNP is not available in your area, another Medicare Advantage plan may be a good fit.

atoms.title: Full versus partial dual eligibility
atoms.question: Who can enroll in a D-SNP plan?
atoms.text: You can enroll in a D-SNP if you are enrolled in both Original Medicare (Part A and Part B) and Medicaid through your state. There are two levels. Full dual eligibility means you receive both Medicare and full Medicaid benefits; Medicare covers most services while Medicaid helps pay copays, coinsurance, deductibles and premiums. Partial dual eligibility means you get support from a Medicare Savings Program (MSP) that helps cover certain Medicare costs without full Medicaid medical benefits. Not all D-SNPs accept partial dual eligibility, so check requirements before enrolling.

atoms.title: How to enroll in a D-SNP
atoms.question: How do I enroll in a D-SNP?
atoms.text: You can enroll in a UnitedHealthcare D-SNP by phone or with an agent, and you can also enroll in some plans online. You need to have both Medicare and Medicaid to qualify.
